articles.title_orig: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China
articles.title_zh: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China
articles.content_orig:
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region
China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.
The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq , Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.
Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”
Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.
When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan , bolstering its status as a regional mediator.
Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”
As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.
Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.
The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.
Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.
Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

articles.title_orig: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.title_zh: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.content_orig:
Yum Brands on Tuesday reported earnings that beat expectations, but a cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell weighed on the company's same-store sales growth.
However, Yum said Taco Bell, which the company considers a "growth engine" for its business, has since rebounded.
"Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the [quick-service restaurant] industry on same-store sales growth," Yum CEO Chris Turner said in a statement.
Shares of Yum rose more than 3% in premarket trading.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Yum reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $1.62 billion, or $5.92 per share, up from $397 million, or $1.41 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut and other items, the restaurant company earned $1.56 per share.
Net sales rose 4% to $2.05 billion.
During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. It closed the sale of the pizza chain's business in mainland China to Yum China on Aug. 7 and sold the rest of Pizza Hut to LongRange Capital on Sept. 1. The company's third-quarter results include Pizza Hut up until those dates.
Excluding Pizza Hut, Yum's same-store sales were flat for the quarter as Taco Bell weighed on the company's overall results. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined by 4% as diners temporarily pulled back on visits due to the foodborne illness outbreak .
Yum executives previously said the weekend of July 18 saw the most severe impact to sales, but sales trends have improved since then.
Outside of the U.S., Taco Bell's much smaller international business reported same-store sales growth of 5%.
KFC's same-store sales ticked up 1%, helped by system sales growth in China and Europe. The U.S., now the chicken chain's third-largest market, saw system sales shrink 6% in the quarter.
Like Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes , KFC has struggled in the U.S. amid a wave of new competitors and more budget-conscious consumers.

articles.title_orig: Pfizer hikes full-year outlook, taps company veteran as new CFO
articles.title_zh: Pfizer hikes full-year outlook, taps company veteran as new CFO
articles.content_orig:
Pfizer on Tuesday reported third-quarter results that topped estimates and hiked its full-year outlook, as demand for its newly launched and acquired products grows.
Pfizer also Tuesday announced that Cecile Guegan , who has held various finance leadership roles at the company over the last two decades, stepped in as chief financial officer this month. She had served as interim CFO since August, when Pfizer's former CFO, Dave Denton, stepped down to take the same position at Nike.
The company is now expecting full-year revenue to total $62 billion to $64 billion, which compares to a previous outlook of $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion. The low end of that sales range would be roughly flat or down slightly compared with 2025 revenue of $62.6 billion. Still, Pfizer cited its "strong year-to-date performance" as a driver for the guidance hike.
The pharmaceutical giant now expects full-year adjusted profit of between $2.95 and $3.05 per share. That compares with a previous guidance of between $2.80 and $3 per share.
That includes a one-time $650 million charge, or a negative impact of 10 cents per share, recorded in the third quarter tied to the company's licensing and collaboration agreement with Chinese cancer drugmaker Innovent Biologics.
Pfizer is working on a comeback story after its massive pandemic-era success waned. As demand for Covid products drops and generic rivals threaten its biggest moneymakers, CEO Albert Bourla is looking to jumpstart growth through strategic acquisitions, fresh cancer drugs and a big bet on weight loss treatments through its acquisition of Metsera.
Pfizer in August expanded its multi-year cost-cutting efforts to help offset sharp declines in Covid product sales, and is now targeting roughly $9.7 billion in net savings through 2029.
Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Tune in at 1:30 p.m. ET as Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla joins CNBC TV to discuss the company's earnings. Watch in real time on CNBC+ or the CNBC Pro stream.
Pfizer reported third-quarter revenue of $16.58 billion, relatively flat from the same period a year ago. The company cited an operational decrease of $57 million, primarily due to lower Covid revenues, and a $15 million negative impact from foreign exchange.
That was offset by strong sales of key products like its blood thinner Eliquis and targeted cancer drug Padcev, which jumped and beat expectations.
Eliquis in particular raked in $2.52 billion in sales, up 25%. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.40 billion, according to StreetAccount. Padcev posted $720 million in revenue for the period, which compares to the $658 million that analysts were expecting.
Sales of Pfizer's newly launched and acquired products grew 32% operationally. That includes Padcev, its respiratory syncytial virus vaccine Abrysvo, its pneumococcal shot Prevnar 20 and oral lung cancer drug Lorbrena, among several other products.
Pfizer's Covid products also topped estimates for the quarter despite seeing steep sales declines. The company's Covid vaccine generated $808 million in sales, which compares to the $770.4 million that analysts were expecting, StreetAccount estimates show. Meanwhile, Pfizer's antiviral pill, Paxlovid, booked $449 million in sales, coming in above the $394.1 million that analysts were expecting.
The company booked a net income of $3.24 billion, or 56 cents per share, for the period. That compares with net income of $3.54  billion, or 62 cents per share, during the third quarter of 2025.
Excluding certain items, including restructuring charges and costs associated with intangible assets, Pfizer posted earnings per share of 87 cents for the quarter.

articles.title_orig: Indian national killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
articles.title_zh: Indian national killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
articles.content_orig:
An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man  killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

articles.title_orig: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
articles.title_zh: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
articles.content_orig:
The stock market is not yet pricing in a Democratic sweep of Congress — despite some polls and most prediction markets pointing that way — so that scenario could weigh on share prices Wednesday, according to investors and analysts.
Republicans managing to keep control could cause a short-term relief rally, they said.
Short-term moves aside, the typical post-midterm pattern in the months ahead is bullish. But some wonder if the market could buck the positive historical trend this time because the S&P 500 is already up so much this year going into the election.
As far as certain stocks to watch, a big Democratic win on Tuesday night — especially in the Texas governor race — could add fuel to an AI stock sell-off on the notion that more data center restrictions would gain momentum nationally. Defense stocks could come under pressure on fears of limits on spending.
Polls are pointing to a Democratic victory in the House and a toss-up in the Senate. Prediction markets have been more favorable to Democrats, calling for a blue sweep .
While investors are signaling "begrudging acceptance" to a base case scenario that there will indeed be a Democratic sweep, that's not how they're positioning, said Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research. The firm's recent survey data among more than 100 institutional investors suggests they are not strongly positioned for any particular result.
"Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests," Marcus told CNBC, noting that the firm shares the view that the "polling is likely overstating Democratic strength."
JPMorgan sees a blue wave knocking the S&P 500 by about a half percent on Wednesday.
On the other hand, if Republicans end up retaining both chambers of Congress, that could spur a rally, said Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
"From a certainty standpoint, the market knows what to do with Republicans holding both chambers," he said.
Citigroup strategists said Monday that Republicans losing the House but managing to keep the Senate could be "a tailwind for equities into year-end." JPMorgan traders predict up to a 1% pop on Wednesday if Republicans hold on to that chamber.
Looking past any short-term move, stocks tend to rally after the midterms have concluded. In fact, the S&P 500 was up one year out after all midterm elections going back to the early 1980s.
But the S&P 500 has already recorded double-digit gains so far in 2026, so some on Wall Street worry that investors are being overly complacent heading into this year's elections.
During midterm election years, the S&P 500 has typically averaged a 14% drawdown at some point in the second half of the year found Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG.
"The reason stocks often perform well in November during midterms is because [the S&P 500] typically is weak INTO the elections. We have the opposite setup this year," Krinsky wrote last week. "Therefore, while consensus is that we see a post midterm rally, we think the opposite is actually more likely."
It's not helping that the broader market has recently come under significant pressure due to turbulence in the AI trade, which led the Nasdaq Composite to post its worst day since June on Friday. AI shares led the market lower again on Monday.
A strong showing from Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections could pressure the trade even more .
At the state level, increased Democratic control is probably a headwind for stocks associated with data centers and technological capital equipment, analysts said.
"It [would solidify] the early kind of cautionary signs in different states around the advancement of AI infrastructure," Rob Rains at Washington Analysis told CNBC.
Goldman Sachs strategists said this week that a Democratic Congress "might limit data center tax incentives, but a national moratorium looks unlikely in any election outcome."
One example would be Texas — a key hub of the data-center buildout. A surprise loss there by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has the "potential to spook" the market in the short term, Wolfe's Marcus said.
A blue wave might pressure defense shares, while boosting health care stocks, analysts and investors said.
"A substantial Democratic sweep could limit real spending growth unless a broader agreement increases both defense and health-care funding," said Alex Sagal, global equity analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. However, he noted that the earnings outlook for the defense industry looks "stable to modestly positive."
Wolfe Research's Marcus said that healthcare is going to be "the biggest focus," as Democrats will push for restoring expired Affordable Care Act enhanced premium subsidies or unwinding some of the Medicaid reforms in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act .
"Healthcare stocks have been doing really well lately," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said to CNBC. "I think part of that is the anti-AI trade, but I also think part of it is just optimism that Democrats are taking over."
Ellerbroek is keeping his eye on hospital-related stocks such as HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare as well as health insurers like UnitedHealth and Centene .
Financials was the worst S&P 500 sector in early 2026 on the heels of President Donald Trump calling on Congress to pass a law that would cap credit card interest rates at 10% . While the sector has been able to notch gains since, with its year-to-date rise now at around 3%, things could get more unstable for the group under Democratic control.
"Democrats will come in wanting to show tangible progress on the affordability issue, and that means targeting sectors that are front and center in consumer budgets," said Evercore ISI's Matthew Aks. "We know Trump has populist instincts, populist leanings, and could he pick a couple of issues and decide to team up with the Democrats on those issues and target those industries in a populist way? Absolutely."
Given that Democratic control is often associated with increased regulation, while Republican control is thought to promote deregulation, Democrats could be interested in passing credit card rate caps if they come out victorious.
"I think if Democrats have control of one or both chambers, they would try to pass it and see if they could get Trump to either sign it or force him to veto it, and that would let Democrats kind of score a political point," Aks said.
Trump could restart the war against Iran after holding off any major strikes leading up to the midterms, a move that could upend the overall market and cause energy stocks to outperform. Crude oil prices jumped more than 10% in October, though they gave a lot of that gain back on Monday.
Gasoline prices stood at $4.17 a gallon on average nationwide Sunday, a nearly 40% increase compared to the same period last year, per AAA.
"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysts at Gas Buddy, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."
If Trump decides to take forceful action, it could snuff out hope for a typical post-midterm year-end rally.
Evercore ISI said the S&P 500 could retreat by double-digits to end the year at 6,800 as oil spikes if the president "moves to kinetic escalation in Iran ahead of seating the new Congress in January" and Democrats take Congress.
— With reporting by Sarah Min, Tobias Burns and Spencer Kimball

articles.title_orig: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
articles.title_zh: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
articles.content_orig:
The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.
Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.
The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic.
"This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.
Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic .
Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.
So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".
Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.
The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.
Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sank to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.
In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%.
"Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.
This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found.
Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".
Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs".
"But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.

articles.title_orig: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
articles.title_zh: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
articles.content_orig:
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.
The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.
The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".
Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.
Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.
It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen .
Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.
As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.
Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".
Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.
Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.
iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn).
Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.
Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.
The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.
Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.
Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood".
Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%.
Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business.
While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive".
However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading.

articles.title_orig: Campaign to keep Ilhan Omar’s secrets safe includes threats against anyone who speaks out: ‘You’ll be killed … snake’
articles.title_zh: Campaign to keep Ilhan Omar’s secrets safe includes threats against anyone who speaks out: ‘You’ll be killed … snake’
articles.content_orig:
Few members of the tight-knit Somali community are willing to talk about Ilhan Omar — due to threats and fear of violence if they do.
The Minnesota representative is backed by a fiercely protective group, many of whom take it upon themselves to bombard anyone who speaks out with online threats and even physical harm in the US, Europe and Africa.
The group is not officially connected to Omar, and do not receive instructions from her and it is unclear if she is personally aware of their actions.
The Post understands one member of the community who broke ranks was assaulted on the streets of Minneapolis and again in Kenya after their name appeared in the press.
The critic was attacked outside a Kenyan restaurant in 2022 and left with a concussion as well as several cuts and bruises.
“I got jumped by 15 people and was pepper-sprayed,” the man, who asked not to be named for fear of further retribution, told The Post.
“After that I don’t really remember what happened. All I know is I was thrown to the ground and had so many punches and kicks thrown at me.
The man believes the attack was sparked by a popular Somali TikTok star, who described the critic as a “fool” and threatened to “punch him in the face” if he ever comes to Minnesota.
“I was attacked because of this man. He set his followers on me after sharing my location,” he claimed.
In separate videos, the TikTokker tells his loyal fans: “There are people in our community who have snitched on Ilhan Omar, as well as gone after her father.
“People have looked the other way for too long, you bitches.”
Local Minnesota journalists have encountered problems reporting on Omar since she was first elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2016. The notoriously protective and tight-knit community was quick to hurl accusations of racism at anything that questioned her background, policies or turbulent personal life , sources told The Post.
Omar first came to Minnesota as a refugee in 1995, escaping the bloody civil war in Somalia. She has faced allegations she fraudulently married her second husband — also her alleged brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — for immigration purposes. They married in 2009 and split around 2012, but did not divorce until 2017.
Meanwhile, one Post source within the community received a chilling phone call, telling him to recant anything he had ever said about Omar and to instead issue statements of support for her ahead of the midterms.
“ I feel very threatened for simply disagreeing with anything to do with Ilhan Omar,” the source claimed.
“If you don’t support her, then these people online really want to make you pay. I am fearful of my life every single day. I wish I never said anything about her.
“I get death wishes every day, and I am afraid to leave my home. On the rare occasions I do, I am verbally abused or, worse, actually physically assaulted.”
Only a handful of people in the Somali community have been willing to publicly share what they know about Omar’s relationship with Elmi since it first came to light.
One man based in Somalia, known as Aardile, claimed to have put a hit out on the Minnesota man who was quoted speaking negatively about Omar in a report.
“We are sending people after you, they’re going to put you in hospital and in a coma,” he proudly stated in a video online.
“My heart sank when I heard that because these people are not a joke, they’re dangerous,” the source told The Post.
“I stayed in bed for the entire week and could not face going outside in fear of being shot dead at any moment.”
Another outright told him “you are going to be killed” and labelled him a “snake.”
The Post also heard a chilling seven-minute phone call made by a “leading member” of the Somali community in the city to someone speaking against the congresswoman.
The source was explicitly told to say “I lied about Omar because we were arguing” and to publish a message of support for her ahead of the elections.
The source — who also asked not to be named — ultimately refused, but said he felt pressured because he didn’t want to be “villainized in the community” further.
None of the social media trolls are linked to Omar and she is not accused of any wrongdoing. Her office did not respond to a request for comment from The Post.
The congresswoman has vehemently denied that her 2009 marriage was a sham to obtain legal immigration status for Elmi.

articles.title_orig: As Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms, Gulf Countries Brace for Possible Renewal of Iran War
articles.title_zh: As Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms, Gulf Countries Brace for Possible Renewal of Iran War
articles.content_orig:
Some Arab states have warned Iran that they could retaliate individually or collectively if Tehran targets their infrastructure, as Persian Gulf countries prepare for the possibility of renewed US strikes and Iranian retaliation, the Wall Street Journal reported Monday.
Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have been conducting security drills, including at airports, while some attendees at a major energy conference in Abu Dhabi were cutting short their stays on government advice. Schools in Riyadh were also set to remain online this week as Saudi Arabia faces attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said his country hoped diplomatic efforts would succeed but was “braced for the worst.”
The warnings come against a backdrop of continuing attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. A tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles near a Saudi port late Sunday, while another vessel was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman early Monday. Iranian state media also reported Monday that an oil tanker caught fire after striking a mine in the eastern part of the strait.
The heightened preparations coincide with diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed fighting. Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday, with a draft proposal still circulating for feedback and a follow-up meeting possible. An Iranian source cited by the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said Monday that indirect communications with Washington had produced no diplomatic breakthrough and that Tehran continued to insist on its seven conditions. A third Qatari delegation in a week was heading to Tehran on Monday as Doha sought to bring Tehran and Washington closer to an agreement to end the war, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported, citing an informed Iranian source.
Axios reported that Qatari mediators had drafted an agreement outlining a three-day sequence of confidence-building measures aimed at resuming direct US-Iran negotiations. Trump told Axios he was “in no rush” to decide whether to resume fighting with Iran, saying: “One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush.” The diplomatic push has also exposed differing views within the Trump administration over how to proceed. CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio favor maintaining economic pressure without either a new war or a deal, while Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are urging Trump to move toward an agreement, Axios reported.
Vance said Monday that Washington had made “some progress” toward a negotiated settlement. “The President and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance said, adding: “We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more.”
Despite those signs of progress, the possibility of renewed US military action remains. The Journal reported that Trump has been leaning toward a large attack on Iran after the US midterm election but has not decided whether to proceed. Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a call Saturday that he wanted to first give continuing diplomatic efforts a chance to succeed, according to people familiar with the call.
“Prime Minister Netanyahu is not pressing President Trump. President Trump knows exactly what he wants to achieve and how he wants to achieve it,” Danny Danon told Al Arabiya English.
“Israel will collaborate with the United States. We will support the decision of the United States, but it is not us pressing anyone,” he added.
Danon’s remarks followed an Axios report Sunday, citing an Israeli and a US source, that Netanyahu was urging Trump to strike Iran immediately after the November 3 elections, while the US president preferred to allow negotiations to continue.
The Israeli source described the leaders’ Saturday phone call as “tough,” while the US source called it “direct.”
Trump confirmed Sunday that he had spoken with Netanyahu about Iran, describing their conversation as “a very good talk,” without providing further details.
Danon also rejected a claim by US commentator Tucker Carlson on X that a nuclear strike against Iran was being considered, calling the idea “delusional.”
“No one is even discussing it in the US, nor in Israel,” he said.
Washington weighs military options and diplomacy
Trump said Saturday that negotiations with Iran were “going fine” and that he was in no hurry to resume military action, although he said Washington still needed to target one or two sites, including the suspected underground nuclear complex at Pickaxe Mountain.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump had not decided whether to launch further strikes.
“He hasn’t made a decision,” Rubio told reporters in Atlanta, adding that Washington preferred to resolve the conflict peacefully.
Rubio said diplomatic contacts had remained active, often through intermediaries, and declined to set a deadline for negotiations.
Iran says diplomatic contacts remain active
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that consultations through mediators, including Qatar and Pakistan, remained intensive, after several days of talks with Qatari officials ended without a breakthrough.
“Everything depends on the political rationality of Washington,” Araghchi said, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.
Araghchi said a revised proposal developed through mediation could allow the Strait of Hormuz to reopen within two days if Washington accepts Iran’s conditions.
Tehran’s earlier seven-day plan called for Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales before negotiations resumed.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Monday that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government “certain authorities” regarding peace talks with the United States, according to IRNA.
Pezeshkian said Iran would seek to resolve the conflict through dialogue, without specifying the scope of those powers.
An Iranian source cited by the Revolutionary Guards-affiliated Fars news agency said Monday that indirect communications with Washington had produced no breakthrough and that Tehran still insisted on its seven conditions for progress. Exchanging messages through intermediaries was routine, the source said.
Despite the diplomatic contacts, Danon said in his Monday interview that Israel remained prepared for military action regardless of uncertainty surrounding the formation of a new government following last week’s Israeli elections.
“The military is prepared, we are ready and if we will need to protect our people, we will do it,” he said.
The country’s dependence on the waterway leaves its gas industry exposed to prolonged shipping disruptions. For state-owned QatarEnergy, buying supplies produced outside the Persian Gulf offers a way to earn trading income when its own exports are constrained.
The new contracts will begin delivering in 2030 or later. They offer protection against future losses, but cannot restore shipments from Qatar’s damaged facilities or reopen its export route.
The risks were underscored on Friday, when a Qatari LNG carrier was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Persian Gulf, the same day Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran aimed at reaching a deal between Iran and the United States.
The Al Mayeda was hit Friday evening, its owner Nakilat said Sunday. No crew members were injured or environmental damage reported, and the vessel remained operational.
Qatar condemned the attack as a “dangerous act” threatening maritime navigation and global energy supplies, saying investigations were underway to identify those responsible.
War exposes Qatar’s dependence on Hormuz
Qatar is particularly vulnerable to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. LNG accounts for half of its foreign-currency export revenues, and shipments to markets beyond the Persian Gulf must pass through the waterway.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's next target: A major shake-up of America's wireless market
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's next target: A major shake-up of America's wireless market
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX ( SPCX ) may be attempting an end run to circumvent obstacles it's facing in getting a mobile network off the ground.
Per the Washington Post , SpaceX is in talks with EchoStar ( SATS ) about launching its own wireless phone service through Boost Mobile, after the country's three biggest carriers — Verizon, AT&T ( T ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) — reportedly turned down SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Musk met with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen last month, according to two people familiar with the negotiations cited by the Post. The talks could end with SpaceX buying Boost Mobile outright or getting access to its network, which the discount carrier leases from AT&T and T-Mobile.
In recent months, Musk asked the heads of Verizon ( VZ ), AT&T and T-Mobile to let SpaceX use their networks for its own mobile service. All three said no, per the Post.
But there may be a catch to SpaceX's plan. Typically, a carrier's lease agreement can't be transferred to a new owner without the host carrier's permission, meaning AT&T and T-Mobile may still need to approve a Boost deal to provide access to SpaceX.
SpaceX is open about its ambitions in the terrestrial mobile space. On the company's recent earnings call , CFO Bret Johnsen said the goal is to "become a major mobile carrier ... in the United States." SpaceX also recently agreed to buy $8 billion worth of wireless spectrum licenses intended for cellular service in places satellites can't reach.
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said on X .
SpaceX and EchoStar already have a relationship. In September 2025, SpaceX agreed to buy EchoStar's AWS-4 and H-block spectrum licenses for about $17 billion, split between up to $8.5 billion in cash and up to $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock, EchoStar said at the time . SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said the deal would "advance our mission to end mobile dead zones."
What SpaceX still lacks is a ground network. Its satellite signal isn't strong enough yet to carry cell coverage indoors or in dense cities, where most phones are - and that's why a deal with Boost would be so crucial.
An MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) like Boost rents capacity on an existing carrier's network. Last month, TD Cowen's Gregory Williams called acquiring an MVNO the cheapest and fastest route for SpaceX to launch mobile service, noting a network build would cost "upwards of $80B" and take years.
The Big 3, he said, still show no desire "to (ever) sign an MVNO deal with Starlink that could ravage the industry."
Carrier executives have publicly doubted that SpaceX can rebuild their tower networks. Verizon's CEO put the build-out at four to six years. Musk said it would take about half that.
"Veterans of the cellular industry look at the chess board of existing pieces and don't see a solution," Musk said recently on X . "They don't understand that SpaceX is developing entirely new pieces that fundamentally alter the strategic landscape."

articles.title_orig: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.title_zh: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.content_orig:
Despite U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix is reportedly being smuggled into China. Smugglers are using a method of packaging HBMs with low-end server processors to bypass export regulations, and then detaching only the memory once in China.
According to the U.S. IT media outlet The Information on Nov. 2 (local time), smugglers who have recently been siphoning Korean HBMs to China are exploiting loopholes in export regulations.
They package the HBM with a low-end server processor on a board and export it to China. They target the fact that while exporting HBM alone is subject to U.S. regulations, packaging it with a server processor classifies the package as a server processor item.
Under U.S. export regulations, the total computing power of a semiconductor package is evaluated based on the server processor, not the memory chip. The packages are disassembled upon arriving in China. Local technicians apply heat to the board to melt the solder, detach only the necessary HBM, and discard the remaining server processors.
The separation process requires highly sophisticated skills. It is reported that the failure rate is high because applying heat too quickly or for an extended period can cause the memory stack to warp or crack.
Nevertheless, the smuggling continues due to the massive profits.
A broker in his 20s who handles HBM smuggling in China told The Information that the price of a single HBM3E, which traded for several hundred dollars just a year ago, has recently soared to about $4,000. A single AI chip package requires 6 to 8 HBMs. The memory price alone amounts to $24,000 to $32,000. AI processors, servers, and power costs are separate.
The HBMs secured in this way are reportedly sold mainly to customers of Huawei, a Chinese telecommunications equipment and IT company.
According to sources familiar with Huawei’s supply chain, Huawei recently explained to some customers that its next-generation flagship AI chip, the Ascend 960DT, will largely be equipped with HBMs produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Huawei introduced that the performance of the Ascend 960DT is twice as superior as existing chips, and it will be one of the powerful processors that China can produce on its own.
As it became difficult to directly purchase the necessary memory chips from Korean companies, Huawei even advised some AI chip ordering customers to secure HBMs on their own. China is clinging to securing Korean HBMs because it lacks its own production capacity.
HBM is a core component that enhances the processing performance of AI processors by quickly transmitting large amounts of data. Without securing enough HBMs, it is difficult for a high-performance AI chip to exert its full performance even if it is developed. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for more than 80% of the global HBM market.
The problem is that such smuggling could also act as a burden on Korean semiconductor companies. Even if Samsung Electronics and SK hynix did not directly violate export control regulations, they could become targets of U.S. government surveillance if Chinese AI chips equipped with their memory are discovered.
In fact, Taiwan’s TSMC was investigated by the U.S. government in 2024 after semiconductors it produced were found in Huawei products. Subsequently, the U.S. ordered TSMC to completely halt AI chip exports to China.
SK hynix stated, “We are strictly complying with relevant laws and regulations, including the export control regulations of the U.S. and South Korea,” adding that it has never supplied products to Huawei since the implementation of U.S. export regulations in 2020.
Meanwhile, a perception is emerging among smugglers who consider their transactions to be a patriotic act.
A broker in his 20s who smuggles memory in China told The Information regarding his work, “It is contributing to the motherland.” He reportedly does not consider himself a smuggler.
However, as smuggling competition intensifies, concerns about crackdowns are also growing.
Another smuggler who has been ordering memory semiconductors from South Korea revealed that the risk of detection is increasing as other brokers have started using the transaction routes he used.
He said, “The more people like us there are, the easier it becomes to be discovered by regulatory authorities,” adding that he plans to sell most of his company stakes next year as crackdowns by South Korea and the U.S. are expected to be further strengthened in the future.

articles.title_orig: Russian attack on Ukraine aid hub kills 31 as US announces new peace talks
articles.title_zh: Russian attack on Ukraine aid hub kills 31 as US announces new peace talks
articles.content_orig:
Russian air strikes kill at least 26 in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region
Russian forces have bombed an aid centre in Ukraine, killing at least 31 people, according to Ukrainian officials, as the United States announced plans for new peace talks on November 10 and 11.
The aid centre, at a school in the village of Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, had been closed to students because the village sits too close to the front line, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday. Instead, it served as a shelter and as a weekly distribution point for aid packages, which residents who remain in the village collected every Monday.
“The Russians struck first just as people were arriving – a few aerial bombs,” he said in his nightly address. “Then there was a second strike – more air bombs, this time on the shelter. A vile terrorist strike.”
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages.
Among the dead were two members of a rescue crew and four police officers, according to Ukraine’s emergency services. Five people, including two rescue workers, were being treated in hospitals.
Photographs posted online showed smouldering debris scattered across the area.
There was no immediate comment from Russia.
Zelenskyy said the attack was “further proof that Russia does not want any kind of de-escalation, any real justice.”
He argued that Moscow had squandered an opening created by a humanitarian mission last week in Oleshky , a Russian-occupied southern city, which was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
“If Russia genuinely wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps,” he said. “We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people.”
Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian intelligence had warned that Russia was preparing a new “massive attack” on the country’s energy and logistics networks, timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Writing on X, he said Moscow was counting on the world’s attention being elsewhere, allowing Ukraine’s struggles with air defences and Patriot missiles to go unnoticed.
He urged Washington to pressure Russia “in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war”.
Hours after the attack, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said that delegations from Ukraine and Russia would meet in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, on November 10 and 11.
In a social media post, Witkoff said the talks would address “post-war security agreements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures, and ending the war”.
Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to the new round of three-way talks after meeting Witkoff in St Petersburg on October 21.
The talks come as US negotiators seek a breakthrough before winter in the war, now in its fifth year.
The last US-mediated talks were held in February, before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, cited Monday’s attack in urging countries to oppose Russia’s return to elite international sport, after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ordered that Russia be reinstated in major ice hockey tournaments.
“Russia deserves condemnation, isolation, and consequences, not a return to international respectability,” Sybiha wrote on X.
Elsewhere in Ukraine on Monday, drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region, damaging a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and homes, according to emergency services. In the Black Sea port of Odesa, five people were injured when a warehouse was hit and nearby houses were damaged.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight. The governor of Russia’s Samara region, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said air defences had repelled an attack there but gave no further details.

NVIDIA's RTX 50 GPUs will be getting more expensive in November, as manufacturers confirm price increases across all models.
All consumer graphics cards have faced price hikes throughout this year , & as we approach the end of 2026, it looks like more price bumps are on the way.
In a report by Chinese sources, it looks like regional manufacturers have more or less confirmed that price increases are on the way. These price increases will be implemented throughout the current month, with lower-end models getting at least $30 US higher while higher-end models being $400 - $500 higher.
If you've been following our reports on GPU price hikes, you would know that these aren't just restricted to NVIDIA's RTX 50 GPUs.
AMD's Radeon RX 9000 and Intel's Arc GPUs, alongside the Prosumer models such as RTX Pro, Radeon AI Pro, and Arc Pro, are also affected. The reason for the price hikes is rising memory prices, which are associated with shortages caused by huge demand from AI, and also elevated costs of other components.
We have already reported how RTX 5090s are being sold for over $7000 (now approaching $10K), RTX 5080s going for over $2000 US , Radeon RX 9070 XTs soon approaching $1000, and Arc Pro B70s also doubling in price.
Starting in November, the price trend for graphics cards is basically confirmed to continue rising, with various brands likely to implement price increases throughout the month.
According to internal sources from AIC (Add-in Card) manufacturers, the cost prices of various graphics card brands are expected to continue rising in November. The RTX 50 series is particularly affected, with high-end models anticipated to see larger increases, estimated at around 1000-2000 yuan, while mainstream models are expected to start at least 200 yuan higher.

articles.title_orig: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.title_zh: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.content_orig:
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.
When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.
But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.
But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.
Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.
Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.
Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".
She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.
That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.
For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.
Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.
All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.
In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.
But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.
Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier .
Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.
Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.
One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.
They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.
One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.
Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.
Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.
Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.
The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed , that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.
In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.
She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.
They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.
But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

articles.title_orig: Israeli opposition unites behind Eisenkot as Netanyahu says voters chose him for PM
articles.title_zh: Israeli opposition unites behind Eisenkot as Netanyahu says voters chose him for PM
articles.content_orig:
Israel's opposition party leaders agreed to work toward forming a "national emergency government" as soon as possible, saying they would act immediately to do so in a joint statement following a meeting on Tuesday.
The leaders of the opposition bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met for the first time since the election, amid disagreements and a political deadlock between the two blocs, with no clear path toward forming a government .
Those attending the Herzliya meeting included prime ministerial candidate Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar), Naftali Bennett (B'Yachad), Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu) and Yair Golan (the Democrats), along with outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid, who holds the second slot on the B'Yachad Knesset slate.
The leaders said they were committed to honoring what they described as a clear voter mandate for change and against the continued tenure of the current government, which they referred to as the “October 7 government.”
“The party leaders are in agreement on the need to establish a Zionist government based on the four principles set out by Eisenkot, as soon as possible,” the statement said. The Yashar leader outlined the four principles on Saturday.
The statement added that the parties’ negotiating teams would begin working immediately to formulate the government’s guiding principles and the agreements for the formation of the 38th government, and to "put the clear parliamentary majority in the Knesset to work."
The party leaders also agreed that all five parties would recommend to President Isaac Herzog that the Yashar chairman receive the first mandate to form a government , with the aim of establishing a new government as quickly as possible and avoiding another election.
In a statement given following the meeting, former prime minister Bennett said Eisenkot had the opposition's full backing to "act as quickly as possible to establish a Zionist government of repair," arguing that the bloc needs to act "with great urgency.
"We have no time. We need to act with great urgency. Therefore, as soon as possible, we will take control of the Knesset, secure the mandate to form a government, and act as quickly as possible to establish a Zionist government of repair in order to bring about a revolution for those who serve and begin repairing the country," Bennett said.
Prior to the meeting, B'Yachad deputy Lapid also stressed the need for the opposition bloc to form a government.
"We are facing a serious and dangerous attempt to undermine the election results. We must form a government ," he said. Netanyahu's Likud has alleged in recent days that there was election interference and that the Arab parties had “stolen” the election.
"The events of the past few days are just another reminder that we need to remove Netanyahu from the Prime Minister's Office," Lapid added.
Victims and family members of those killed in the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks arrived outside the meeting of party leaders to demand that they form a government to replace Netanyahu.
"You have a mandate. Do not lend a hand to legitimizing the leaders who were at the helm during the October 7 massacre. Establish a change government," they stated.
"The people voted no confidence in the October 7 government and gave 67 seats to the demand for change. You have received a mandate. Do not waste it on compromises that would legitimize those who were at the helm on October 7," they added.
The meeting comes amid numerous disagreements between the party leaders, although all have agreed to recommend Eisenkot, whose party won the most seats within the opposition bloc, to President Isaac Herzog as the candidate to form the next government.
Consultations at the President's Residence are set to begin on Wednesday. By law, the president is required to consult the Knesset factions before deciding who receives the task of forming a government.
Golan has called on the opposition party leaders to form a government with the Arab parties - Ra'am and the Joint List - who won a record-breaking 19 seats combined in the elections. With Arab parties, the opposition bloc would have a Knesset majority of 67 seats.
However, Liberman reiterated on Tuesday ahead of the meeting that a coalition with the Arab parties was not an option. Bennett had also drawn a red line ahead of the elections against forming a government with the Arab parties.
The opposition bloc lacks the required 61-seat Knesset majority without the support of the Arab parties. The election results showed that Netanyahu’s bloc maintained its lead, securing 53 seats in the next Knesset, while the opposition bloc won 48.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations. Other possible outcomes include a unity government between Netanyahu and members of Eisenkot’s bloc , or a minority government.
Liberman also said on Monday that he opposed both a minority government and a unity government with Netanyahu.
Meanwhile, the Arab parties have expressed willingness to cooperate with the opposition bloc to replace Netanyahu.
The meeting between the opposition party leaders also comes amid debate regarding who to select as the candidate to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, who is a member of Netanayhu's Likud.
Opposition party leaders have reportedly agreed that their first move after the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10 would be to oust Ohana.
The move would require a majority in a Knesset vote and could be achievable with the support of the Arab parties, bringing the potential backing to 67 seats.
Replacing Ohana would give the opposition bloc greater control over the parliamentary agenda, including votes, legislation, and committee appointments, even if Netanyahu remains in office as head of a caretaker government.
The Knesset is expected to be sworn in on November 10, regardless of any government or coalition talks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere.
The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes.

"We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
"The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked."
Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda .
ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA
Ukraine's largest private energy company reports 90% of generation capacity damaged by Russian attacks, leaving over 1 million without power during freezing temperatures. (Reuters)
In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences.
"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned.
"We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added.
"We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left talks with President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet during a lunch meeting at the White House on Oct. 17, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner , both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow.
Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy.
The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters.
The proposed sale could provide a significant boost to Ukraine's air defenses if finalized, although the delivery timeline is uncertain.

Nearly 800 people were evacuated during the six-day humanitarian pause, according to first lady Melania Trump, with the White House clarifying that she helped broker the arrangement.
Ukraine's General Staff accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian pause to rotate troops, reinforce their defenses and improve battlefield logistics.
"Under the ceasefire introduced for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of the Defence Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said in a statement on X.

Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.
However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.
Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.
With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.
Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.
When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.
These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.
The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.
Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.
Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.
This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.
At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.
This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning, too.
Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night.  Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.
Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.
The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.
The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.
To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards).
The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.
Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.
Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.

articles.content_orig:
Aramco reported a 9% rise in third-quarter adjusted net income on Tuesday on stronger refining margins.
The Saudi oil giant posted adjusted net income of $31.2 billion for the quarter, up from $28.6 billion a year earlier. The figure exceeded the median analyst consensus estimate of $30.66 billion, according to the company.
Aramco's downstream business, which processes crude oil into fuels and other products, posted adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of $10.3 billion, up 234% from a year earlier, driven by stronger refining margins.
"Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security," Aramco CEO Amin H. Nasser said in a statement.
Nasser said the company's operational flexibility and supply network enabled it to continue delivering energy to customers despite the disruptions. Aramco is also exploring additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to strengthen its global supply network.
The company generated $28.2 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, up from $23.6 billion a year earlier.
Aramco said its board declared a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, up 3.5% year on year, to be paid in the fourth quarter.
The company also said its major upstream projects remained on track and highlighted its acquisition of a 49% stake in Saudi artificial intelligence company HUMAIN.
– CNBC's Emma Graham contributed to this story.
